newsitem.title: UK: Moslems told to vote selectively in UK election.
newsitem.headline: Moslems told to vote selectively in UK election.

text.p: A British Moslem body said on Thursday that British Moslems should vote in the forthcoming election for candidates who best address their concerns about religious discrimination and promise funding for their schools.
The UK Action Committee on Islamic Affairs (UKACIA) urged Moslems to question candidates about their views on these issues at a news conference called to launch a booklet on its priorities.

"Traditionally, Moslem support has been with the Labour Party, but at the moment there's not one particular party that addresses all the key concerns of the community," said Iqbal Sacranie, a joint convenor of UKACIA.

He estimated that there were as many as two million Moslems in Britain, most of them British-born with family roots in Pakistan, India and Bangladesh. Between 500,000 and 750,000 were eligible to vote in the election, due by May, he added.

There are currently no Moslem members of parliament. Sacranie could not say how many Moslems were standing this time as candidates for one of the major parties, but he said at least one was a Labour candidate in a safe Labour seat in Glasgow.
Sacranie said the UKACIA was opposed to Moslems standing for parliament as independents because, on past form, such candidates would attract very few votes.
Instead, Moslems should push their concerns through the main political parties.

"Action on some of these concerns, for example on legislation to deal with religious discrimination and the elimination of double standards on the question of funding for Moslems schools, is urgent," the UKACIA document said.
The UKACIA says Christian and Jewish schools attract state funds, but Moslem schools do not, even when they satisfy the educational standards for such religious schools.

Candidates who oppose Britain's National Lottery would be recommended by UKACIA. "The lottery is having a massively detrimental impact on the lives and health of millions of people, encouraging false expectations and attitudes to individual worth, effort and achievement," it said.

The UKACIA speaks for a network of mosques and community associations, and claims to be representative of British Moslems. But 30 or so people were protesting noisily about its voting advice outside the news conference at London's Islamic Cultural Centre.
They said they were representatives of a "mainstream" association, Al-Muhajiroun, which believes the Koran forbids Moslems from voting in a non-Islamic state.
